sections.html:
Clark County lies along the Ohio River, facing Louisville from the Indiana side. Jeffersonville serves as seat and biggest city, while Clarksville, Charlestown, Sellersburg, Henryville, Marysville and Speed turn up on deeds all the time. The 2020 census put the county at 121,093 residents and Jeffersonville at 49,447, a jump driven partly by annexation.

Annexation matters at tax time. Two houses a mile apart can sit in different taxing districts, and the bill stacks county, municipal and school levies together. Look up your parcel's district before you compare your bill with a neighbor's.

Water and wind shape what buyers ask about. The tornado outbreak of March 2012 hit Marysville and Henryville hard, so a house there may have been rebuilt, and an inspector will want permits and repair records. Near the river or a creek, buyers will also ask about flood coverage, so keep elevation certificates and any damage paperwork where you can find them.

Inside Jeffersonville, a parcel may sit in Port Fulton, the historic area where the Howard Shipyards once stood, in Oak Park, annexed in 2008, or near the downtown riverfront around Big Four Station. Each pocket draws different buyers. The Big Four Bridge walking and cycling crossing has made the riverfront a destination, and homes near it often draw more interest than the same house farther inland.

Jobs feed the housing market here. River Ridge, built on the former Indiana Army Ammunition Plant land, now houses manufacturing, aerospace, food and beverage, life sciences and logistics firms, and Interstate 65 has pulled subdivisions and shopping centers along it since the 1950s. The old Jeffboat yard closed in 2018, and the city has talked about redeveloping that 80-acre riverfront site. Workers at Norton Clark Hospital, the schools and the National Processing Center fill many of the nearby rentals and starter homes, which is helpful to know if you are selling a landlord property.

Two installments make up the year. The usual due dates are May 10 and November 10, and paper bills go out in early April. Pay Copy A in spring and Copy B in fall. If a due date lands on a weekend, the state calendar pushes it to the next business day.

Walk-in payments go to the treasurer at 300 Corporate Drive, Suite 105, Jeffersonville. The counter is open Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., with a break from noon to 1 p.m., and the phone is 812-285-6205. To pay by mail, send the right copy of the bill with a stamped, self-addressed envelope to PO Box 1689, Evansville, IN 47706, and you will get a receipt back.

Some local banks take payments in collection season too. They want the bill in hand, an account with no delinquency, and payment by the due date.

An appeal starts with Form 130, filed with the assessing official, one petition for each parcel. The cutoff is June 15 of the year the county mails the assessment notice. When no Form 11 goes out, the cutoff is June 15 of the year the bill is mailed. Read the notice you received for the exact date.

The assessor sets up an informal meeting first and sends the outcome to the Property Tax Assessment Board of Appeals. That board has 180 days from the petition to hold a hearing and must mail notice at least 30 days beforehand. Skipping the hearing without a valid continuance or withdrawal can cost $50. Not happy with the board? File Form 131 with the Indiana Board of Tax Review.

Come to the meeting with proof. Sales of comparable houses nearby, an appraisal, and photos or estimates for needed repairs all help. Tidy paperwork carries more weight than a general complaint that the number feels high.

Parcels with delinquent taxes can go to a tax certificate sale run by the Clark County Treasurer. The winning bidder gets a lien in the form of a Tax Sale Certificate issued by the County Auditor.

After the sale the owner has a year to redeem by paying what Indiana Code requires, interest included. If nobody redeems, the bidder can ask for a tax deed. The sale list is posted at sriservices.com. Bidders are advised to talk to a lawyer, and owners facing the list should do the same.

Before the sale stage, a late payment costs 5% of the delinquent tax when it arrives within 30 days and the parcel has no earlier delinquency. In all other cases the charge is 10%. A house that is headed for the list can often be sold first, which stops the balance from growing.

sections.h2: Selling a Clark County house with taxes due
sections.html:
Deferred repairs, inherited houses and landlord exits are the usual reasons Clark County owners sell fast, and each brings its own tax questions. Work through this list:

  • Ask the treasurer for today's balance before you pick a closing date.
  • Fill out the sales disclosure form. Indiana requires it before the deed goes to the county auditor.
  • Collect permits and storm repair records if the home is near the river or in a tornado-hit area.
  • If you used the homestead deduction, a buyer who closes after the assessment date can claim it by December 31 of the purchase year.

Unpaid tax does not stop a sale. The title company takes the balance out of your proceeds at the table. A cash buyer can skip showings and repairs, and the title company still settles the tax from your proceeds.

Two habits save trouble. First, get the payoff from the treasurer in writing and hand it to the title company. Second, keep the bill itself, since the office asks for Copy A or Copy B with any payment and charges $1.00 per parcel for a duplicate. If a due date passes before you close, a penalty of 5% or 10% can attach, and a quick closing often costs less than a long listing.

If the property is inherited, the tax bill may still show the former owner. Tell the treasurer's office and the closing agent early, bring the estate papers, and confirm the mailing address so notices reach the person who is actually handling the sale. When the house has a tenant, the bill and the due dates do not change, so build the next installment into your closing figures. And if the home sits in a flood-prone spot or was repaired after the 2012 storms, line up the permits and receipts a buyer's inspector will ask about, since a clean file helps the sale close on schedule.

A realistic timeline looks like this. In the first week, call the treasurer for the balance, request the deed history, and decide whether repairs are worth doing. In the second week, collect offers and pick a closing agent. Before closing, confirm the payoff again, because penalties and the date of payment move the number. At closing, the agent pays the tax, records the deed, and hands you the net. Keeping a copy of each receipt in one folder makes the last step easy, especially if a buyer's lender asks for proof of payment.

faqs.q: When do Clark County property taxes come due?
faqs.a: Usually May 10 and November 10. Copy A of the bill covers spring and Copy B covers fall, and bills typically mail in early April.

faqs.q: Where can I pay in person in Clark County?
faqs.a: At the treasurer's office, 300 Corporate Drive, Suite 105, Jeffersonville, Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., closed noon to 1 p.m. Mail goes to PO Box 1689, Evansville, IN 47706.

faqs.q: How long can I redeem after a Clark County tax sale?
faqs.a: One year from the sale date. After that the bidder may ask for a tax deed, and redemption means paying the statutory amounts plus interest.

faqs.q: What is the Clark County appeal deadline?
faqs.a: June 15 of the year the notice or tax bill is mailed, filed on Form 130. Use one petition per parcel and read your Form 11 for the exact date.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Clark County house that has back taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The title company pays the balance from your proceeds at closing. Get a payoff figure from the treasurer first, since a 5% or 10% penalty may apply.
